newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals - Tough Japan aluminium talks foreseen.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals - Tough Japan aluminium talks foreseen.

text.p: Tough haggling is expected in talks later this month to set Japanese aluminium premiums for the July-September quarter, given uncertainty over Japan's economy after last month's sales tax rise, traders said on Wednesday.

"This time sellers are bullish. There'll be tough negotiations as we can't gauge demand for the second half," said a trader at a major trading house. "The key is the reaction to the sale tax increase on April 1."
Japanese trading houses and large end-users are to begin talks over third-quarter supply contracts around May 19.
Traders agreed that third-quarter premiums would likely be below current high levels of about $90 a tonne as they expect an increase in supply, including new production at Australia's Boyne Island.

But some were worried the premiums might settle at around $82, like the long-term contracts for the second quarter, against a backdrop of strong U.S. demand, lower LME warehouse stocks and firm U.S. Midwest premiums.
"I can't imagine premiums going much below the levels seen for the second quarter," said a second trader. "It's difficult as we are at a turning point after a tax hike."
Japan increased its national sales tax to five percent from three percent on April 1.

In one of the first indicators of future demand, the Japan Automobile Dealers' Association said last Thursday that vehicle sales in Japan fell 12.7 percent in April from a year earlier to 326,975 units -- the first drop in eight months.

However, industry leader Toyota Motor Corp said it expected its sales to bounce back quickly, helped by planned new models and large potential demand for cars to replace those bought in Japan's late-1980s bubble economy era.
Metals traders said they were waiting to see economic data for May and June to get an indication of likely future demand.

The physical copper market has been quiet in the past week, though nominal premiums slipped to $60/70 pre tonne in line with narrowing backwardation in London and an increase in LME warehouse stocks since late last month, traders said.
High copper prices had deterred China from picking up the metal even though its stocks seemed to be running low, they said.
"China is eyeing $2,300 per tonne. It's too expensive now," said a trader. "But they have large buying interest. You can see it also in falls in stocks in Singapore."

On Tuesday, Bankers Trust in London predicted Chinese copper consumption was likely to sharply exceed most estimates, eroding stocks and pushing prices to $2,866 per tonne by the end of 1997 -- compared with $2,360 of three months in London at kerb close.
Japan's spot zinc market remained quiet after heavy imports expected to cover most of its needs under the Generalised System of Preferences scheme last month, traders said.
"It's very quiet. China is keen to sell the metal but they can't find any buyer here," a zinc trader said.
